Age / Sex:         24 months / Male
Race / Ethnicity:  Not documented / Not documented
Insurance:         Not documented
Language:          English

A 24-month-old boy is brought to clinic by his father after a fall at home.

About 2 hours ago he fell off the living-room couch onto a hardwood floor. Father was in the kitchen and heard the thud; the boy was crying when he got to him. He vomited once in the car on the way in. No seizure activity. Immunizations up to date. No drug allergies. Weight 12.8 kg. Otherwise healthy.

Exam: alert, walks to the toy bin and plays, GCS 15. HR 112, RR 24, SpO2 99% RA. 3 cm soft boggy swelling over the occiput, no step-off, no laceration. Pupils equal and reactive. No hemotympanum, no Battle sign, no periorbital bruising. Fontanelle closed. No bruising elsewhere on full skin exam. Neuro non-focal, gait normal. Remainder of exam unremarkable.

What is your plan?
raw_text:
Analyzed query, searched for evidence

Practice Guideline

The American College of Radiology (ACR) classifies acute minor pediatric head trauma by PECARN risk category, and for this child places CT in the "may be appropriate" but not routinely indicated tier — structured observation is a reasonable alternative to immediate CT.

At 24 months, this boy is evaluated under the PECARN ≥2 years algorithm. He has a GCS of 15, normal mental status, and no signs of basilar skull fracture, so he is not high-risk. His single episode of vomiting is an intermediate-risk predictor (history of vomiting), placing him in the intermediate-risk group, where the estimated risk of clinically important TBI is ~0.8%. 
American College of Radiology
[1]
 For this group the ACR states that CT and clinical observation are competing reasonable strategies, and that CT may be favored over observation in the setting of parental preference, multiple risk factors, worsening symptoms or signs during observation, or in young infants where observation is more difficult. 
American College of Radiology
[1]
 With an isolated single risk factor and a reassuring, stable exam, observation is appropriate. 
American College of Radiology
[1]

If he had met very-low-risk criteria — GCS 15, normal mental status, no basilar skull fracture signs, no LOC, no vomiting, no severe mechanism, and no severe headache — CT would not be recommended. 
American College of Radiology
[1]

American College of Radiology

ACR Appropriateness Criteria® Head Trauma-Child.

Expert Panel on Pediatric Imaging, Ryan ME, Pruthi S, et al. Journal of the American College of Radiology : JACR. 2020;17(5S):S125-S137. doi:10.1016/j.jacr.2020.01.026.

Recommended plan: observe rather than immediately image. This 24-month-old meets the PECARN ≥2-year pathway (occipital scalp hematoma is only a predictor in children <2 years, so it does not upgrade his risk here). 
JAMA Pediatr
 + 1
[2-3]
 His only intermediate-risk feature is one episode of vomiting; with GCS 15, a non-focal neuro exam, normal gait, and reassuring behavior (playing, walking), his risk of clinically important TBI is well under 1%, and most such children can be safely managed without CT if observed. 
JAMA Pediatr
 + 2
[2-4]

Specific steps:

Observe in clinic/ED for ~4–6 hours from the time of injury, with serial neuro checks (mental status, pupils, tolerance of oral intake). Emesis after pediatric head trauma is common and, when isolated and non-progressive, correlates poorly with intracranial injury. 
Pediatrics
 + 1
[4-5]

Proceed to non-contrast head CT if any deterioration occurs during observation: recurrent or persistent vomiting, worsening or persistent headache, increasing lethargy or irritability, any focal deficit, or seizure. A post-traumatic seizure should lower the CT threshold substantially. 
American College of Radiology
 + 1
[1][4]

Shared decision-making with the father regarding CT vs. continued observation, factoring in his comfort with monitoring and ability to return quickly. 
American College of Radiology
[1]

Skin/NAT screen — already reassuring. A fall from a couch is a plausible, consistent mechanism for an occipital hematoma at this age, the history is internally consistent, and the full skin exam shows no additional bruising. No specific findings raise concern for abusive head trauma here, but documentation of mechanism, developmental plausibility, and the normal skin survey is warranted (PECARN rules do not apply to suspected abuse). 
Pediatrics
 + 1
[4][6]

If imaging is obtained and shows an isolated, non-displaced skull fracture with a normal neuro exam, hospitalization and neurosurgical consultation are generally not required — such children can be discharged to a reliable caregiver. 
Pediatrics
 + 2
[7-9]

Discharge criteria and caregiver instructions: discharge once he has tolerated oral intake, remained at GCS 15 with a stable exam, and has a reliable caregiver. Provide written return precautions: repeated vomiting, worsening/persistent headache, increasing sleepiness or difficulty waking, confusion, unequal pupils, clear fluid
